notes.title: Patch #3 – Survivor Mode is Here!
notes.content:
Hi everyone,

Patch #3 is live, and it’s our biggest update so far! This update brings bug fixes, polish, and quality-of-life improvements, but the real highlight is something many of you have asked for: a brand new game mode – Survivor Mode.

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/4ca914a04e351d6984a7bbdc5d8bff9d6137a15e.png"]
What is Survivor Mode?
Survivor Mode is all about jumping straight into the action. Instead of building up a base and slowly preparing for waves, you’ll be thrown right into the fight:

You start with a Mech at its lowest upgrades, armed only with the Katana sword.



Alien waves begin immediately and keep getting tougher with new enemy types and higher intensity.

There’s no base building here. Instead, you’ll need to clear alien nests to unlock upgrades and new weapons.

Survivor Mode also features exclusive Orbital Strike weapons that can’t be found anywhere else.

And if you manage to survive long enough… the final boss will appear. Beat it, and you’ve conquered the run.

This mode is designed for those of you who wanted a faster, more action-packed experience, while Classic Mode remains for players who love the more strategic, colony-building gameplay.
Other Updates in Patch #3
Bug fixes for stability and smoother play.

Quality-of-life improvements across the board.

UI, audio, and balance polish.
A Note from Me
I’m beyond excited to finally share Survivor Mode with you all. It’s been a long road getting here, and your feedback has been an essential part of shaping this game. If you’re enjoying it, please consider leaving a Steam review—it helps me out so much as a solo developer.

And of course, come join us on Discord to share your feedback, bug reports, and survivor stories. I can’t wait to hear what you think of the new mode!

See you out there,
Nima

notes.title: Optimization, Polish, and the Joy of Digital Photography
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

This week, the pace of adding new features has intentionally slowed down. Instead of introducing more mechanics from my backlog, I’ve been focusing on testing, polishing, and optimizing the existing systems. This approach ensures that I don’t accidentally introduce new bugs or impact FPS performance negatively, especially as we get closer to release.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/272c67dc4428a12446bfdb76030e9f1caea5974a.png

Optimization: Cutting What Doesn’t Add Enough Value

A big part of this week’s work has been hunting for FPS-impacting elements that don’t bring enough value to justify their performance cost. It’s a tough process—some of these features took a lot of time to develop, but with some distance, I can now evaluate whether they truly enhance the gameplay, atmosphere, or overall experience.

The goal is clear: make the game run better while keeping the core experience immersive and enjoyable for all players, including those on lower-spec computers.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/9f8e0a097f055b87b486f8f9920be46e781bcac5.png
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/d0d01f397f32e0b3274b5be3ae72610d5f4a888e.png

Photo Mode: A New Appreciation for the Worlds

I’ve also found myself using the Photo Mode more and more, sometimes stopping in the middle of a battle or after spending time building up my base just to capture a moment. This feature is turning out to be one of my favorites, and I hope others will enjoy it just as much.

Not only does Photo Mode add a nice change of pace between intense waves, but it also offers a new way to explore and appreciate the worlds. Since it allows for free camera movement, players can see the landscapes from a fresh perspective—something that isn’t possible in the usual top-down gameplay.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/618ed8d4462c7efe362fce7d1efc59a2d97d6f6c.png

Looking Ahead

With the focus on polish and performance, I’m making sure the game feels great to play before adding new content. There’s still a lot to refine, and I’m excited to keep improving the experience.

If you haven’t yet, join the Discord to share your feedback, ideas, or even some in-game photos—I’d love to see how you’re using Photo Mode!

Thanks for being part of the journey—see you next week!

It’s been a few weeks since my last update, but I haven’t really taken a break from developing Wave Defense: Trappist. Over the holiday period, we released the second patch to the demo, a major update focused on optimization and the introduction of the Photo Mode.

We also did a deep dive into the game’s music, crafted by legendary electronic musicians Joel Mull and Nima Khak (me!). If you haven’t already, check it out—it’s one of my favorite parts of the game!

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/25755edcc0edcd3baadf1a91ef7170de9849f6e7.png

UI Rework and HUD Improvements

The game’s HUD has been revamped with two main goals in mind:
[olist]
 Minimizing screen clutter, giving players more room to enjoy the world and action.
 Clearer, faster access to key information.

 The minimap is now circular, moved to the lower-right corner, and becomes semi-transparent when not hovered over.
 Stats and resource values have been moved to the right side of the screen, freeing up the lower center for a cleaner view.
 Added projected credits and crystal gains from buildings after each wave, a feature requested by players.

The Pause Menu has also received a significant upgrade with four new tabs:

 Perks Overview: Displays perks selected at each XP level.
 Mech and Weapon Stats: Shows detailed values for the current loadout, making it easier to see the effects of selected perks.
 Building Breakdown: Offers an in-depth overview of all buildings and related stats, helping players make informed strategic decisions.
 Photo Album: Players can view all the pictures they’ve taken in Photo Mode.

Revised Tutorial and New Lore

Additionally, I’ve added some lore and background to explain why the player is in the Trappist system and the importance of collecting crystals. While I won’t spoil too much here, I’m excited to continue developing this aspect of the game and hope it adds depth to the overall experience.

New Settings for Performance Optimization

To help players on lower-end computers, I’ve introduced a new Downsampling option in the settings menu. This allows players to slightly lower the game’s graphics, which can significantly improve FPS without drastically affecting visuals. In my tests, even small adjustments made a noticeable difference. If you’re experiencing FPS drops, this is worth trying!

Bug Fixes

Here are a few bugs that have been resolved in this update:

 Fixed an issue where photos taken in-world weren’t saving to players’ computers.

 General stability and optimization fixes.

Looking Ahead

It feels great to kick off 2025 with so many exciting updates and improvements already in place. As always, your feedback is invaluable, so keep it coming! Join the Discord to share your thoughts, report bugs, and suggest new features—I’d love to hear from you.

notes.title: Crafting the Soundscape of Wave Defense: Trappist
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

This week, I want to shine a spotlight on the music and sound design of Wave Defense: Trappist, an area that is absolutely crucial to the atmosphere and overall experience of the game. To help tell this story, I’m thrilled to share insights from none other than Joel Mull, the world-renowned electronic musician who has written and produced the majority of the game’s music and sound.

A Creative Collaboration Between Two Sci-Fi Enthusiasts
In spring 2023, a creative partnership began between two friends and Sci-Fi enthusiasts—myself and Joel Mull. At the time, Wave Defense: Trappist was about six months into development. While the game already had a visual identity and some placeholder sound design, Joel saw an opportunity to elevate the project with a truly unique and personal soundscape.

The collaboration quickly grew from an idea into a shared vision. Inspired by our mutual love for Sci-Fi classics like Alien, Dune, and Blade Runner, we began to shape the narrative and atmosphere of the game together.

Exploring the Story and Themes
One of our earliest discussions revolved around the idea of why the Mech—a central figure in the game—was on this alien planet. This brainstorming led to an intriguing concept: a mysterious monk order from the 1100s, sent to exploit the planet’s resources and ship them back to Earth’s factories.

But the story didn’t stop there. The planet itself fights back, as its local creatures see the Mech as a threat to their environment and survival. This layered narrative creates a sense of conflict and introspection, blending action with deeper themes of exploitation and resistance.

Crafting the Soundscape
The shared vision for the game’s visual style and narrative became the foundation for its sound and music. Joel began experimenting with an incredible mix of sacred choirs, ambient textures, synths, and electronic elements to capture the game’s tone.

notes.title: New Music, Mech Rework, and Weapon Overhaul
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

This week has been all about introducing some of the big systems I’ve been planning for Wave Defense: Trappist. From music and mech improvements to a full weapon overhaul, there’s a lot to share! Let’s dive in.

New Music by Joel Mull

As a music producer myself, sound design and music are a huge part of the world I want to create in Wave Defense: Trappist. That’s why I’m so thrilled to announce that Joel Mull, the world-renowned electronic music producer, has written and produced brand-new tracks specifically for the game.

The addition of Mull’s music is a game-changer, bringing a deeper atmosphere and energy to every battle, exploration, and build session. I’ll be dedicating a future update entirely to this topic, and hopefully, I can get Mull to share some of his thoughts directly with you all. Stay tuned—this is just the beginning of a much bigger story around the game’s music!

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/b9b4deb5d6a60fa53ab3f8b8d80fe96dcd678f94.png

Mech Movement Rework with Inverse Kinematics

One of the biggest changes this week is a full rework of the Mech’s movement and animations. I’ve implemented Inverse Kinematics (IK), which, without getting too technical, means the Mech’s movements are now far more realistic and dynamic.

Previously, the Mech’s weapon would simply spin in its hand when aiming, but now, the Mech’s entire body and arms move naturally as it adjusts to aim at different targets. This makes controlling the Mech feel much better, whether you’re walking, running, jetpacking, or shooting at enemies.

This system has been a lot of work to get in place, but I’m confident it makes a noticeable difference to the feel of the game. I’ll continue to refine and improve this system with each iteration, and I can’t wait to hear your feedback on how it feels.

Weapon Overhaul and New Weapon Stats

The game’s weapons and weapon systems have received a major overhaul this week. Each weapon now has a distinct feel thanks to the introduction of a Weapon Handling stat.

Some weapons, like the Radioactive SMG, are fast and nimble, while others, like the Gatling Gun, are harder to handle but deal massive damage. To give players an easier overview of weapon differences, each weapon now displays three core stats:

 Damage – How much raw damage the weapon deals.
 Handling – How easy and smooth the weapon is to use.
 Efficiency – How resource-efficient the weapon is in battle.

All weapons in the game have been rebalanced to reflect these changes, making them feel more unique and satisfying to use.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/15eb46ac3775b35c95740e74897f5de8d1f35c42.png

New Weapon: The Staff Cannon

I’m also excited to introduce a brand-new weapon: the Staff Cannon. This will be an endgame weapon, designed to be both incredibly powerful and very fun to use. It’s perfect for players who want to bring some serious firepower to the battlefield!

At the same time, I’ve decided to remove the Fire Bow, as it no longer felt like it fit with the game’s overall design. And as a final touch, the Flamethrower now has its proper weapon model, adding a polished look to one of the most satisfying weapons in the game.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/cc880433080f455ecef801e3d08714855088d85e.png
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/6a306e47505dea25ee47063104bcbc7f9efc1828.png

Bug Fixes and Miscellaneous Improvements

Finally, here are some additional updates and fixes that went into the latest build:

 Feedback Form Fixes: Resolved issues with the feedback form to ensure smoother player input.
 Audio Mixer: Fixed a bug that caused the audio mixer to not work correctly when players were in the world.

Looking Ahead

It’s been a busy but exciting week of development, and I feel like the game is moving closer to the vision I’ve always had for it. With new music, improved Mech animations, and a refined weapon system, Wave Defense: Trappist is shaping up to be more dynamic, immersive, and fun than ever.

As always, your feedback is invaluable, so please let me know what you think of the new changes. Join our Discord to share your thoughts, report bugs, or suggest features you’d like to see in the game.

Thank you so much for your support—see you next Week!

Feedback from Playtests: Polishing the Pause System

One key issue reported by testers was the game’s pause and unpause behavior, which was acting strangely in certain scenarios. During my own testing, I tended to stick to the "Happy Path" (doing things as intended), so I never triggered these bugs myself. Thanks to the feedback, I was able to identify and rebuild the logic for how and when the game pauses.

The new system ensures the game will pause correctly when players:

 Open the map
 Receive an upgrade
 Send feedback or report a bug
 Interact with other menus or systems mid-game


This rebuild has made the pause system much more robust and should feel much smoother and more intuitive for players. It’s a small but important improvement that enhances the polish and makes a better first impression for new players.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/5ed49ef3d3d066a1c9660938fa45b02760b7d7a5.png

 The Start Menu
 The Mech Construction Hub
 Mid-game while deployed on a new world


This change makes it easier for players to customize their experience without interruptions, no matter where they are in the game.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/d41fb2bec2b767054ccf4badd09df5ba7769e7f1.png

Introducing the Companion Drone

 Automatic Combat Support: The drone replaces the Mech’s old "passive auto weapon" system. It will now automatically target and shoot at aliens within its range, adding a more dynamic and engaging feel to combat.
 Artifact Scanning: Instead of the Mech’s backpack holding scanning tools, the drone will now be responsible for scanning and detecting Artifacts as you explore new worlds. This makes much more sense visually and thematically.
 Building and Upgrading Structures: When constructing or upgrading buildings, the drone will handle the physical construction instead of structures simply appearing. This small change adds a lot of immersion and polish to the base-building process.


Not Just a Helper, but a Friend

One of the things I love most about the drone is the emotional element it adds. Landing on a new planet used to feel a little lonely, especially before your base was set up. Now, with the drone by your side, you’ve got a companion to share the adventure with from the start.

notes.title: The Final Boss Fight, UI Updates, and Upcoming Demo
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

Welcome back to another dev blog for Wave Defense: Trappist! This week has been packed with exciting work on the game’s endgame content, specifically the final boss fight that players will encounter after navigating the path of worlds we talked about last week. I’ve also been tackling some UI adjustments to improve the base-building experience based on feedback, and I’m thrilled to announce a demo coming in December!

The Final Boss Fight: The Ultimate Challenge

When players reach the end of the procedural map and overcome all the challenges along the way, they’ll be met with one last, ultimate test—the final boss fight. This encounter is designed to feel very different from the other worlds and battles players have experienced. Here’s what makes it unique:

  No Base-Building: Unlike the other worlds, where players build and defend a base, the boss fight throws players straight into a head-on battle. You’ll be up against a new boss alien that’s significantly stronger and more challenging than any enemies you’ve encountered before.
 Waves of Previous Enemies: To raise the stakes even further, waves of previously defeated aliens will also join the fray. This final battle will test not only your Mech Build but also your Mech Piloting skills under intense pressure.
 Permanent Defeat: One key difference here is that you don’t have a Mission Control building in this battle, which means if your mech is destroyed, it’s game over for that run. There’s no reassembly—only a definitive challenge to see how far your build and skills can take you.


{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/a99e69ceb488005cc627dc50f2951bc0a2901773.png

Designing this boss and creating new abilities and attacks that feel fresh and impactful has been a really fun process. I can’t wait to see how players react to this final showdown and what strategies they bring to the fight!

UI and Base-Building Mechanics Improvements

In addition to the final boss, I’ve also been working on refining the UI and mechanics for base-building. Recently, several playtesters shared feedback that the base-building interface could feel a bit overwhelming, with too much information shown at once. Another issue was the accidental one-click building upgrades—players sometimes upgraded buildings without meaning to, which could disrupt their strategy and resource management.

To address this feedback, I’ve made two key changes:

 Condensed Building Info: Now, when you hover over a building, you’ll see a more streamlined summary. For the full details, you just need to right-click on the building. This change keeps the UI cleaner and more intuitive, while still providing in-depth information when you need it.
 Upgrade Confirmation: Instead of a single button press, upgrading a building now requires you to hold down the button for a few moments. This should prevent accidental upgrades and give players a bit more control over their decisions.


{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/ef8a2fb4cc1e00c940465f3f480266195698246a.png

These changes were designed to make the base-building experience feel more accessible and intuitive, and I’m eager to hear what players think about the updates.

Demo in December!

Now for some big news: with my friends at Caketown, who are publishing the game, we’ve decided to release a demo in December! My focus over the next few weeks will be to polish and stabilize the game to ensure a smooth, satisfying experience for everyone who will try it.

The demo will of course be available here on Steam, so if you’re interested in joining, make sure to wishlist the game and join the Discord to stay up to date with all the details. This is a great opportunity to try the game firsthand, share your feedback, and be part of shaping Wave Defense: Trappist.

However, if you can’t wait for the demo?! Check out this post on how to become an early MECH, joining the beta tester channel on Discord.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/604adeb2c873d596487b4e147dc10ba96152cb32.png

notes.title: Garbage Collection, Autumn Cleaning, and Shooting Animations
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

Welcome back to another update on the development of Wave Defense: Trappist! This week has been a busy one, with a focus on improving the game’s performance, doing some "autumn cleaning" of old assets, and polishing up the shooting animations. Let’s dive into what’s been going on!

Tackling Garbage Collection and Loading Times

As Wave Defense: Trappist has grown, I’ve noticed that the loading times have been getting longer, especially when starting up the game. This was becoming a bit of a concern, so I decided it was time to dig into what was causing the delays.

After investigating, I found that some objects were causing memory leaks, which were contributing to the extended loading times. This was a new area for me, so I spent a good amount of time reading up and watching tutorials on how to use tools like the Memory Profiler to better understand what was happening under the hood.

With the insights gained, I started implementing changes aimed at optimizing how memory is used, ensuring that unnecessary objects are properly cleaned up—essentially working on better garbage collection. While I haven't solved everything yet, I’m happy to report that the loading times have been cut in half compared to before. This feels like a solid achievement for this iteration, and I’ll continue refining it to make sure everything runs as smoothly as possible.

Autumn Cleaning: Tidying Up the Scenes

While working on the loading times, I took the opportunity to do some autumn cleaning across all of my game scenes. Over time, I’ve tested countless game objects, 3D models, and snippets of code, many of which ended up not being used in the final version of the game. Even though these objects were turned off, they were still lingering in the scenes, adding unnecessary complexity.

So, I rolled up my sleeves and went through every scene to delete and clean up anything that wasn’t needed anymore. This kind of maintenance work might not sound glamorous, but it’s incredibly important. Removing unused assets reduces clutter and makes the game more efficient, while also making future updates and iterations much easier to manage. It feels good to have everything cleaned up, and I’m already noticing how much smoother it is to work on the project now.

Shooting Animations: Adding That Extra Polish

Another highlight of this week has been working on shooting and reloading animations for most of the weapons in the game. This has actually been one of the more fun tasks I’ve taken on recently. Animations can make such a big difference in terms of how the game feels, and I wanted to ensure that the shooting mechanics in Wave Defense: Trappist are as satisfying as possible.

Wrapping Up the Week

notes.title: Lighting, Graphics, and the Influence of Moebius
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

I’m back with another dev blog, and this week, I want to talk about something that has a huge impact on the overall feel and atmosphere of Wave Defense: Trappist—the lighting and graphics. Recently, I’ve been working on reworking the lighting in all of the game’s worlds, and I’d love to share some of the challenges, breakthroughs, and inspirations behind that process.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/77c75d0c618bc234178e07c01664dc216f5274f7.png
Reworking the Lighting
Lighting plays such a crucial role in how a game looks and feels, and I realized that the lighting in Wave Defense: Trappist needed a bit of a revamp. This has been one of the more challenging tasks I’ve taken on recently, mainly because I had to really dive deep into learning about lighting—not just in games, but also in movies and TV. I spent hours reading up and watching tutorials and talks on how to light a scene effectively, and then had to figure out how to apply those techniques in Unity, the game engine I’m using to build the game.

One of the biggest technical challenges with this process is that lighting in Unity requires baking, which essentially means locking in the light and shadows for each scene. This takes time, as I have to bake the light for every world in the game and then recompile all of the shaders that are used. It’s a time-consuming process, but the end result has been totally worth it.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/6f4385597298aedbccfbf3d8fe221661981518d5.png
A Chance to Revisit Each World
While reworking the lighting, I took the opportunity to revisit each world and reflect on the original artistic vision I had for the game. One of the biggest visual inspirations for Wave Defense: Trappist is the comic art of Jean Giraud, better known as Moebius. Moebius had such a unique and vibrant style, with clean lines, surreal landscapes, and bright, otherworldly colors that create a sense of wonder and adventure.

As I revisited each world, I realized that some of them had drifted a little too far into “functional” design—where the focus was purely on gameplay without enough attention to the visual harmony of the world. By referencing Moebius' work again, I could see where some of the worlds needed to be adjusted to align more with the coherent, vibrant art style I want the game to have.

For example, some worlds that had harsher, darker tones were reworked to feel more colorful and light, in line with Moebius’ playful use of pastel colors and bright, dreamlike skies. This process allowed me to refine the game’s overall visual style while keeping each world unique and distinct.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/d2771f327ae633f76b60b7d8184d3a19505be74a.png
Technical Challenges and Performance Considerations
While I was excited to push the graphics and lighting further, one of the key considerations throughout this process was performance. I wanted to make sure that the game’s visual improvements wouldn’t come at the cost of smooth gameplay. As I made changes to the lighting and shaders, I constantly monitored the game’s performance to ensure that players would still get a seamless experience without any major hits to frame rates.

It’s been a balancing act—finding that sweet spot where the game looks great, feels cohesive with the rest of the world, and still runs efficiently. I’m really happy with the progress so far, but this is definitely something I’ll continue to iterate on, especially as more feedback comes in.

The Influence of Moebius
I want to take a moment to dive deeper into how Moebius’ work has influenced the visual design of Wave Defense: Trappist. Moebius was known for his ability to create these fantastical, alien worlds that felt both familiar and utterly strange at the same time. His use of color, light, and surreal landscapes had a huge impact on how I envisioned the different planets and biomes in the game.

What I admire most about Moebius is how he could evoke such a sense of wonder and exploration through his use of bright, almost pastel-like colors and clean, minimalist lines. His work has this incredible balance of simplicity and depth, and I’ve tried to channel that same feeling into the game. Each world in Wave Defense: Trappist has its own distinct vibe, but they all share that sense of exploration and discovery, much like Moebius’ illustrations.

By revisiting these visual influences while working on the lighting, I feel like the game’s look has been significantly elevated. It’s brighter, more vivid, and more cohesive overall, and I hope it creates the same sense of adventure that Moebius’ work has inspired in me.

There’s still plenty of work to do, and I plan to keep iterating on the lighting and visual design as I go forward. But for now, I’m excited about where the game’s visuals are headed, and I think the recent changes have given the game a visual lift without sacrificing performance.

notes.title: Making Your Mech Truly Yours – Customization in Wave Defense: Trappist
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

Welcome back to another dev blog for Wave Defense: Trappist! This week, I want to talk about a feature I’m really excited about—how you can make your mech feel truly personal. Customization is a big part of the game, and I’ve spent a lot of time working on ways to ensure that your mech reflects your playstyle and personality.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/0ad547d58b318e66e2ca5021cebddf089f7f04b3.jpg
Customization Beyond Weapons
In Wave Defense: Trappist, your mech is your main tool for surviving the waves of alien enemies and gathering precious Crystals. While players will have the ability to equip and modify various weapon systems—a topic I’ll dive into in a future blog—there’s another layer of customization that I think will really resonate with players: the ability to paint and customize the appearance of your mech.

With an infinite number of spray cans, endless color options, and a wide variety of brushes, players can spend as much or as little time as they want designing their mech’s look. Want to slap on a quick color change before heading into battle? Easy. Prefer to spend hours perfecting a detailed, multi-colored design? Go for it! You’ll be able to save your paint jobs, meaning that you can return to your favorite designs again and again—or try something new each time.
I believe that this is going to be a feature many players will appreciate. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if some players end up spending more time painting their mechs than venturing out into new worlds to gather Crystals!

The Challenge of Developing Fine-Grained Customization
From a development perspective, this has been one of the more difficult features to implement. The core idea sounds simple—let players paint their mechs—but offering the kind of fine-grained control I wanted for this feature was much more complex than I initially thought.

I spent a lot of time researching different ways this could be implemented, from real-time texture mapping to creating a system that allows for true brush-like precision. I wanted players to feel like they could really take ownership of their mech’s design, whether they were going for a sleek, monochromatic look or an intricate, layered design.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/88ec40b099f2b7ef7e85490415bbd834382513d7.png
Early iterations didn’t give the player the control I was aiming for. The painting tools were too simplistic, and it didn’t feel like the kind of customization experience I wanted for Wave Defense: Trappist. After testing several different approaches, I landed on a system that finally gives players the level of control they need to really make their mechs their own. There’s still room to iterate and improve, and I’m excited to see how players respond to this feature once they get their hands on it.
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/7126e7519e421b59e7357106ef17b06655de538d.png
Designing a Fun and Accessible UI
Another big challenge with this feature has been creating a UI that’s both accessible and fun to use. I want the painting process to feel intuitive, so players aren’t struggling with the controls, but also deep enough that players who want to invest more time into customizing their mechs have the tools they need.

I’ve gone through several iterations of the UI, testing different layouts and control schemes to find something that works for a wide range of players. Whether you’re using a mouse and keyboard or a gamepad, the painting system should feel natural and responsive. That said, the UI is something I’m sure I’ll continue to tweak as more feedback rolls in. Your input will be invaluable in helping me fine-tune this feature, so I’m looking forward to seeing how you all engage with it.

Why Personalization Matters
Giving players the ability to customize their mechs is about more than just aesthetics—it’s about letting them express themselves in the game. I want players to feel connected to their mechs, and one of the best ways to do that is by giving them the tools to make their mech look exactly how they want it to. It’s your mech, your way, and I’m really excited to see the creative designs that players come up with.

notes.title: Crafting the New Player Experience in Wave Defense: Trappist
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

I’m back with another update on the development of Wave Defense: Trappist. This week, I’ve been focusing on something really important—the new player experience. As a developer, one of my biggest goals is to make the game as accessible and enjoyable as possible for new players, while still retaining its depth and complexity for those who want to dig deeper.

While Wave Defense: Trappist is designed to be easy to pick up and play, it also has some layers of complexity. Between piloting your mech, managing the in-game economy, building your base, exploring different worlds, finding artifacts, and navigating the roguelike meta progression, there’s quite a bit to learn. So, this week, I’ve been experimenting with different ways to make the onboarding process smoother and more intuitive.

The First Approach: In-Game Tips
Initially, I wanted to keep things minimal and non-intrusive. My first idea was to provide notifications that would appear during a regular run. These notifications would give players hints and tips as they played, offering guidance on how to use the game’s systems.

However, after testing this approach with a few friends who hadn’t played the game before, I quickly realized it wasn’t working as well as I had hoped. When you’re being attacked by waves of aliens, having text pop up with helpful tips can be overwhelming—too much to process at once! Players found it difficult to absorb the information while also trying to survive the chaos of combat.

Going Back to the Drawing Board
After seeing how hard it was for new players to catch on with the in-game tips approach, I decided to take a step back and really think through what new players need to know to have a good time in Wave Defense: Trappist.

I mapped out all of the key systems and mechanics they’d need to understand: how to pilot the mech effectively, base-building basics, understanding the in-game economy, what to expect from alien attacks, and even the roguelike elements like meta progression. Once I had everything laid out, it became clear that a more structured introduction was necessary.

The Solution: Tutorial World
With this in mind, I decided to create a completely new Tutorial World. This will be the first stop for every new player when they start their first run. In this environment, players are introduced to the game in a more controlled, less stressful setting.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/712a16211249b81c6a7e205f35d58b675f00412f.png
Here’s how it works:

 Meet the Instructor: In Tutorial World, players are greeted by an instructor who guides them through the key mechanics. This guide will walk players through the basics of the HUD, show them how to place down buildings, and provide a solid introduction to the in-game economy and resource management.
 First Taste of Combat: Players will even experience their first alien wave attack in a low-pressure environment. This gives them a chance to test out their mech’s weapons and get comfortable with how combat works before the real challenges begin.
 Mech Construction Hangar: Once the basics are covered, players will be introduced to the Mech Construction Hangar, where they’ll learn about meta progression and how they can improve their mech between runs. This part of the tutorial will be a deep dive into customizing and upgrading their mech—something I’ll go into more detail about in a future blog!
 First Run: After completing the tutorial, players are sent off on their first mission—essentially a normal run—armed with the knowledge they need to tackle the game’s systems and survive the alien onslaught.


Iterating on the Experience
Of course, this is just the beginning. I’m going to continue testing and iterating on the Tutorial World to make sure it strikes the right balance between being informative and engaging. There’s always room for improvement, and I want to ensure that new players feel confident and excited when they start their journey through the Trappist system.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/fa9ceb2f5c980a5598280bdfef2aaf1771bd9105.png
Why This Matters
Getting the new player experience right is crucial for any game, especially one with as many moving parts as Wave Defense: Trappist. By offering a smooth introduction to the game’s mechanics, I hope to reduce any barriers to entry and help players hit the ground running. I’m really excited about the progress so far, and I think this new approach will help players better understand the game and feel more connected to their mechs and their strategies from the start.

As always, I’d love to hear your thoughts! How do you feel about the new Tutorial World approach? Are there any specific mechanics or systems you think should be explained in more detail? Let me know in the comments or on Discord.

Thanks for reading, and see you next week!

notes.title: Behind the Scenes – Redesigning Base-Building in Wave Defense: Trappist
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

Welcome back to the third dev blog for Wave Defense: Trappist. Today, I want to take you behind the scenes of development and give you a glimpse of the redesign process that’s currently underway. As a solo developer, I’m constantly iterating on ideas, testing mechanics, and rethinking how the game plays to ensure it’s both fun and challenging. Lately, I’ve been focused on redesigning one of the game’s core mechanics: base-building.

The Old System: Limited Placement
When I first started working on Wave Defense: Trappist, the base-building system was fairly rigid. The player could only construct buildings in specific locations that I had predetermined. I would place markers across the map, and each marker had a designated building type that could be constructed there. While this gave me a lot of control over the layout and pacing of each level, it also felt a bit restrictive for the player.

Many of you have expressed an interest in having more freedom to choose how and where you build your base, and I totally agree that this would add a whole new layer of strategy to the game. After all, one of the joys of a game like this is the ability to experiment with different setups and playstyles.

The New System: Player Freedom with Base-Building
So I’ve been hard at work redesigning the base-building system to give you more control. In this new version, you’ll be able to build any facility—whether it’s a Power Plant, Trade Post, Droid Factory, or Manufacturing Plant—wherever you see fit. This gives you the freedom to craft your own strategies based on the situation at hand.

Want to create a heavily fortified zone around your Mission Control Facility? Go for it. Prefer to spread out your structures and create smaller, more specialized outposts? That’s also an option! The choice is yours, and I can’t wait to see the creative ways players will experiment with base layouts.

Challenges: Pathfinding and Balancing Freedom
Of course, with more freedom comes more complexity, and this redesign isn’t without its challenges. One of the biggest hurdles I’m facing right now is enemy pathfinding. In the previous system, the AI always knew exactly how to get to your buildings because they were in fixed, predictable locations. Now that the player has more freedom to build anywhere, there’s a risk that enemies might not be able to find their way to certain structures, making them impossible to attack.

This would create an unintentional loophole where players could potentially place important structures in “safe zones” that are unreachable by enemies, breaking the balance of the game.

The Current Solution: Restricted Building Zones
To solve this, I’m implementing a system where areas that enemies can’t pathfind to will be marked as restricted zones for building. These zones will appear as visually distinct areas, and the player won’t be able to place any structures there. Outside of these restricted zones, though, you’ll have complete freedom to build anywhere you want. This way, we maintain the challenge of defending your base from enemy attacks while still giving you a lot more flexibility in how you set things up.

Iterating and Testing
This kind of redesign is an iterative process, and I’m currently in the thick of testing different configurations. I’m tweaking the AI to ensure they can still navigate the environment and attack effectively, while also fine-tuning the balance to make sure that base-building feels fun and strategic without giving players too much of an advantage.

Another thing I’m focusing on is making sure the user interface for this new system is clear and easy to use. Building should feel intuitive, and restricted zones need to be obvious enough that players can immediately understand why certain areas are off-limits without disrupting the flow of the game.

What’s Next?
Moving forward, I’ll be continuing to test and refine this new system, but I’m excited about the direction it’s heading in. Giving players the freedom to design their base layouts opens up so many new strategic possibilities, and I believe it’s going to make base-building one of the most engaging aspects of Wave Defense: Trappist.

As always, I’d love to hear your feedback! How do you feel about having more freedom in base-building? What challenges or opportunities do you think this will present? Let me know in the comments or on Discord—I’m always eager to hear your thoughts!

notes.title: Mastering Base-Building in Wave Defense: Trappist
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

I’m back with another dev blog, and today I’m excited to dive into one of the most strategic aspects of Wave Defense: Trappist—base-building. Whether you’re fending off relentless alien waves or strategically mining precious resources, your base is the heart of your operations. Let’s take a closer look at how you’ll establish and fortify your base in the Trappist solar system.

Building Your Base: Mission Control Facility

Every new world you land on begins with constructing your Mission Control Facility. This building is the nerve center of your base, and it’s crucial to protect it at all costs. If your Mission Control Facility falls, your current run is over, so prioritizing its defense is key to survival.

But it’s not just about defense. The Mission Control Facility also generates Credits, the game’s primary currency, and unlocks Building Zones. As you upgrade this facility, more Building Zones become available, giving you space to expand your base with additional structures.

Critical Facilities and Their Functions

As you develop your base, you’ll have access to various facilities, each with a unique role. Here’s a rundown of what you’ll be working with:


 Power Plant: This facility is the backbone of your base’s energy production. Every other facility relies on energy to function, so running out of power can be catastrophic. Defensive turrets will stop firing, and resource production will grind to a halt. Ensuring a stable energy supply is essential, so consider building and upgrading Power Plants early on. 
 Droid Factory: The Droid Factory produces droids that assist in base defense. These droids can either follow you around or guard specific areas. However, the Droid Factory is a power-hungry facility, so make sure you have a solid energy infrastructure in place before constructing it. 
 Trade Post: The Trade Post is a vital economic hub for your base. It converts harvested resources into Credits by trading with off-world markets. These Credits are crucial for building and upgrading your other facilities. As you upgrade the Trade Post, you can increase trading capacity, improve trade rates, and unlock specialized trade missions, all of which enhance your economic growth. 
 Mining Facility: Crystals are the most valuable resource in Wave Defense: Trappist. Mining Facilities harvest these crystals from patches you discover on each world. The Crystals serve as the main meta-currency, allowing you to make permanent upgrades to your Mechs and other facilities. Like the Droid Factory, Mining Facilities consume a lot of energy, so be prepared to invest in your power grid if you want to maximize Crystal production. 
 Laser Turrets: These defensive structures are your first line of defense against alien waves. Laser Turrets automatically target and attack any enemies within range, making them indispensable for keeping your base secure. Placement and upgrading of Laser Turrets will be critical in holding back the increasingly challenging waves of enemies.



Strategic Upgrades

Each facility can be upgraded using Credits, and these upgrades will enhance their effectiveness in different ways:

  Power Plants will produce more energy and become more efficient, reducing their vulnerability to enemy attacks.
  Droid Factories will increase the number of droids they produce and unlock advanced droid types. 
 Trade Posts will increase trading capacity, improve trade rates, and unlock specialized missions. 
 Mining Facilities will improve the rate at which they harvest Crystals and increase their energy efficiency. 
 Laser Turrets will get a boost in range, damage, and rate of fire, making them even more deadly against incoming threats. 

These upgrades allow you to tailor your base to your preferred playstyle and the unique challenges of each world you explore.

Balancing Defense and Resource Management

One of the core challenges in Wave Defense: Trappist is finding the right balance between defending your base and expanding your economy. Building too many defensive structures might leave you without enough resources to upgrade your facilities, while focusing too much on resource production could leave you vulnerable to enemy attacks. Every decision counts, and the strategic depth of base-building is something I’m really excited for you all to experience.

In the next dev blog, I’ll be discussing the waves of enemies you’ll face and the strategic gameplay involved in fending them off. Until then, I’d love to hear how you plan to structure your base. Will you focus on strong defenses or a robust economy? Let me know in the comments or over on Discord!

As always, don’t forget to join our community to stay up to date with the latest news and connect with fellow players. Thanks for reading, and see you next Wednesday!

If you want to get a closer look and talk directly to me, join my Discord!

notes.title: My story - From music producer to product manager to game developer!
notes.content:
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45097607/087d686571c7ea532e549e95bfbec102a62ba0e9.png

Hey everyone!

A little over a year ago, I was laid off from my job as a product manager. Instead of jumping back into the corporate world, I decided to take a leap of faith and pursue something I’ve always been passionate about — game development. It was a terrifying but exciting decision, especially since I had to start from scratch, teaching myself how to code and use Unity.

After countless late nights, frustrating bugs, and small victories, I’m thrilled (and a bit nervous) to share that my first game, Wave Defense: Trappist, is nearly ready for launch. It’s a roguelike tower defense game where you command a customizable mech to defend your base while exploring the Trappist solar system. Honestly, it’s been a wild ride bringing this world to life.

Here’s what you can expect:
[olist]
Mech Customization: I wanted to give players the freedom to build their own badass mechs, from weapon loadouts to aesthetic tweaks. Every run can feel different depending on how you kit out your mech.
Strategic Gameplay: You’ll need to think on your feet, balancing resource gathering with base defense as waves of alien enemies try to take you down.
A Killer Soundtrack: I was lucky enough to collaborate with techno artist Joel Mull, whose music brings an intense, immersive vibe to the game.
Moebius inspired art style: I've been drawing a lot of inspiration from Jean Giraud's playful and varm palette he used when designing this game. 
[/olist]

If you’re into games that challenge you to think strategically while letting you blow stuff up in a cool mech, I’d love it if you would join our community! Thanks for reading, and I’d be happy to answer any questions about the game or my journey into game development. It’s been a crazy year, but I wouldn’t trade it for anything.

I will continue to post dev blogs every Wednesday so stay tuned! ;)
